extracted.intended_audience: researchers, systematic reviewers, health policy analysts and clinicians studying publication bias and trial reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of empirical reasons, case studies and outcome-classification used to evaluate non-publication, selective publication, suppression and acceptance patterns of clinical trial and conference abstract results. The page aggregates survey/cohort findings and illustrative cases to identify factors that influence whether study results are published and how published reports may differ from full data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of time / other resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Not enough time; lack of time/other resources; too busy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated across multiple surveys/cohorts as a dominant reason for non-publication (e.g. Hartling: 'Not enough time (n = 39): 56.4%'; Weber reasons: 'Not enough time: 74 (41%)'; Vuckovic‑Dekic: 'Not enough time: 10 (48%)'). Often reported alongside 'low priority'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript in preparation / submitted / under review
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors report the manuscript is in preparation, submitted, or under review as reason for non-publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears in many studies (e.g. Camacho lists 'Manuscript in preparation', Krzyzanowska: 'Manuscript in preparation: 5 (13%)', and multiple cohorts report 'Manuscript submitted' or under review). May reflect delay rather than permanent non-publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relocation or loss of authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Author relocation or author moved/passed away causing non-submission or non-publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited explicitly in several surveys as a reason (Camacho: 'Relocation of authors'; Krzyzanowska: 'Author moved or passed away: 4 (4%)').

rubrics_metrics.name: Study incomplete / ongoing with intent to publish
rubrics_metrics.description: Study incomplete or still ongoing, with authors indicating eventual intent to publish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cohorts list 'Incomplete study' or 'Study ongoing' (e.g. Camacho 'Incomplete study'; Sprague: 'Study ongoing: 8 (11%)'; Dickersin lists 'Analysis in progress: 14.7%'). This is frequently distinguished from permanent non-publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results considered not interesting / not important / low priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors judged results as unimportant, not interesting to readers, or gave publication a low priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported as 'Unimportant results', 'Results considered not interesting', 'Low priority' across studies (e.g. Camacho, Hopewell: 'Low priority or too busy: 9 (24%)', Weber: 'Results not important enough: 21 (12%)').

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection by journals / fear of rejection / low likelihood of acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscript previously rejected or authors believe journals are unlikely to accept the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported as 'Rejection from peer-reviewed journal', 'Thought journals unlikely to accept' (e.g. Camacho, Weber: 'Thought journals unlikely to accept: 35 (20%)'). Sometimes conflated with 'manuscript submitted but not accepted'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-author problems / authorship responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems with co-authors (lack of participation, disagreement, responsibility for manuscript belongs to a co-author) that impede submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'Too much trouble with co-authors', 'Co-author responsibility or lack of participation' (Hartling: 'Too much trouble with co-authors (n = 38): 28.9%'; Sprague: 'Responsibility for manuscript belongs to a co-author: 14 (20%)').

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological limitations / poor study quality / design or sample size problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived or actual methodological weaknesses, poor study quality, small sample size, or design problems reduce likelihood of submission/publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as reasons such as 'Low likelihood of acceptance because of methodological limitations', 'Study quality poor', 'Problem of study design', 'Methods inadequate/sampling insufficient' with variable frequencies (e.g. Sprague, Weber, Rotton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other papers with similar findings / duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors cite other published papers with similar findings as reason for not publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears as 'Other papers with similar findings already published' or 'Different version published' (e.g. Hartling, Sprague). May reflect perceived redundancy lowering priority for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-significant or negative results leading to non-publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistically non-significant or negative results cited as reasons for non-publication or delayed publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly reported: 'Results were not statistically significant', 'Negative results' and listed proportions in some samples (e.g. Dickersin: 'Non-significance: 60% in one sample'); also appears as 'Results not positive' or 'Statistical analysis was not positive'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsor interest, intellectual property and patent issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponsor's interests, patent applications, negotiation and IP ownership impede or delay publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blumenthal et al. report 'Patent application submission: 46%','Protection of scientific lead: 31%','Patent negotiation: 26%','Resolution of intellectual property ownership: 17%'. Case studies and examples (appendix 16) illustrate company actions to suppress or delay publication for commercial reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisation or sponsor prohibition / legal threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Organisations or sponsors prohibit publication or threaten legal action to suppress results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases include companies taking legal action (e.g. Olivieri/deferiprone), blocking access to data (Millstone et al.), or threats over guideline drafts (Shuchman). Such actions are documented as causes of non-publication or suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective publication / selective outcome reporting / discrepancy between abstract and paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective reporting of favourable results, omission of unfavourable data, or abstracts whose conclusions are inconsistent with main outcome data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple case examples: celecoxib (6‑month favourable data published; unfavourable 12‑month data unpublished), rofecoxib (omission of myocardial infarctions), gabapentin (internal intent to publish only favourable results), and Alasbali et al.'s finding of inconsistent abstract conclusions in industry-funded studies (18/29) vs non-industry (0/10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delayed publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication is delayed for years after study completion, sometimes until external pressure or inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: alteplase negative results not published for 6 years; ezetimibe results released only after US Congressional inquiry. Documented as 'Delayed publication' or 'Selective (or delayed) publication' in case listings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry sponsorship as a source of publication-related bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Pharmaceutical companies or industry research sponsorship identified as a source of suppression, selective publication, delayed publication or biased reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix 16 lists many cases (e.g. Deferiprone, levothyroxine bioequivalence, statins, Remune, rofecoxib, celecoxib, SSRIs in children) where company sponsorship is linked to non-publication, suppression, selective reporting or withholding unfavourable data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome classification for studies submitted to journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification used in acceptance analyses: 1) Statistically significant (p < 0.05) for primary outcome; 2) Statistically non-significant; 3) Unclear / not analysable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by Olson et al., Lee et al., Lynch et al., Okike et al. to categorise manuscripts and calculate acceptance rates. The page provides proportions of manuscripts in each category and subsequent acceptance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance rates by result type (evidence of possible outcome‑dependent acceptance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed acceptance rates for submitted manuscripts stratified by whether primary results were statistically significant, non-significant or unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Olson et al. acceptance 20.4% for significant vs 15.0% for non-significant; Lee et al. found 4.9% (significant) vs 6.4% (non-significant) with multivariate ORs reported; Lynch/Okike report mixed patterns by specialty. These data are used to assess whether positive results are more likely to be accepted for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrepancy between regulator/submission data and published reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between data submitted to regulators or internal company documents and what is published in journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by examples: unpublished 12‑month celecoxib data less favourable than 6‑month published data; rofecoxib trial omitting myocardial infarctions that occurred after a cut‑off; independent analyses from litigation revealing higher mortality. These discrepancies are flagged as evidence of selective reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisational/administrative prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Organisations explicitly prohibiting publication (e.g., sponsors, institutions) as a cause for non-publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported frequencies in some surveys (e.g. 'Organisations prohibited publication: 9%') and included in qualitative case descriptions of withheld reports.
